phenomenon.name: Djinn
phenomenon.subcategory: Islamic supernatural beings (third created order alongside angels and humans)

description.summary: An order of supernatural beings in pre-Islamic Arabian religion and in Islam, created (according to the Quran) from smokeless fire. Jinn possess free will, can be Muslim or non-Muslim, and constitute one of the three created orders alongside humans and angels. Western 'genies' are a literary distortion of the tradition.
description.full: Jinn (singular jinnī; English djinn) are supernatural beings of pre-Islamic Arabian religion incorporated into Islam as one of three created orders alongside humans (created from clay) and angels (created from light). According to the Quran, jinn were created from a 'smokeless fire' (mārij min nār, Q. 55:15) and are subject like humans to divine judgment, with free will to obey or disobey God. Jinn live alongside humans, generally invisible, and inhabit ruins, deserts, mountains, marketplaces, and human dwellings. The Quran devotes a full surah to them (Sūrat al-Jinn, Q. 72), in which a group of jinn hear the Prophet Muhammad recite and embrace Islam. Iblīs, identified in Q. 18:50 as 'one of the jinn' who refused to bow to Adam, becomes the leader of the shayāṭīn (devils). Classical Islamic sources (al-Jāḥiẓ, al-Damīrī, al-Suyūṭī) and modern studies (notably Amira El-Zein, Islam, Arabs, and the Intelligent World of the Jinn, 2009) describe a typology of jinn including Marid (powerful, often associated with the sea), Ifrīt (powerful and often malevolent), Ghūl (wilderness and graveyard dwellers), Si'lā (female shape-shifters), and Jānn (least-powerful class). King Solomon (Sulaymān) is held to have been granted authority over the jinn (Q. 38:36–38) and to have used them to build temples and works. The Western 'genie of the lamp' figure, popularised by 18th-century European translations of One Thousand and One Nights and especially by the tale of Aladdin (added to the Galland edition c. 1710 from the dictation of Ḥannā Diyāb), gives only a distorted picture: free-will-bearing, religiously-accountable jinn are not the same as Western wish-granting spirits, and the 'three wishes' motif is largely a Western literary invention. Belief in jinn remains an article of mainstream Sunni and Shi'a Islamic doctrine; rituals to seek refuge from jinn (taʿawwudh) and to expel jinn from the possessed (ruqyah) remain part of contemporary Islamic religious practice.

etymology.origin: Arabic root j-n-n (ج-ن-ن), meaning 'to cover, conceal, hide'. Cognate with Aramaic ginnāyē 'tutelary spirits' and possibly with Greek/Latin genius.
etymology.first_use: Attested in pre-Islamic Arabic poetry (e.g. of al-Aʿshā) and central to Islamic scripture from the early 7th century CE.

taxonomy.subtype: Free-willed created order alongside humans and angels

coloration: invisible by default; reported manifestations vary widely

features.description: Quranic doctrine (Q. 15:27, 55:15) holds that jinn are made of mārij min nār, 'a smokeless fire'
Jinn ordinarily cannot be seen by humans; manifestations are reported in tradition but not normative
Tradition holds that jinn may appear as snakes, dogs, scorpions, or humans, especially at threshold places

physical.morphology: Generally incorporeal; classical sources describe them as inhabiting bodies of subtle fire.

abilities.description: Default state, except when intentionally manifesting
Especially into snakes, black dogs, and human form
Held by classical and contemporary Islamic tradition to be possible; treated through ruqyah
The jinn ʿIfrīt of Q. 27:39–40 offers to bring the throne of Bilqis to Solomon before he can rise from his seat
Jinn can be Muslim, Christian, Jewish, polytheist, or unbeliever, and are accountable like humans

patterns: Live in parallel societies with their own families, religions, and tribes
Mingle with humans incognito, especially in transitional spaces and times
Are sought (illicitly) by some practitioners through grimoires and incantations
May be expelled from human bodies through ruqyah (Quranic exorcism)

range.description: Belief in jinn is universal across the Islamic world and present in regions of pre-Islamic Arabian religious continuity. The jinn appear in folklore from the Maghreb to Southeast Asia.

first_recorded.source: Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry; Quranic revelation (early 7th century CE)

peak_activity_periods.description: Quranic revelation establishes jinn as a normative Islamic category
Major classical Arabic literature on jinn (al-Jāḥiẓ, al-Damīrī, al-Suyūṭī)
Antoine Galland's French translation of the Mille et une nuits introduces 'le génie' to European readers
Western horror cinema's 'djinn' genre and increased academic study (notably El-Zein, 2009)

origins.cultural_roots: Pre-Islamic Arabian religion, in which jinn were tutelary spirits of place, war, and poetry; integrated and reinterpreted by Islam.
origins.earliest_accounts: Pre-Islamic Arabic poetry (al-Aʿshā, ʿAntara, Imru' al-Qays); Quranic revelation (Sūrat al-Jinn, Q. 72; passages in Q. 6, 15, 27, 34, 38, 46, 55).
origins.folklore_connections: Closely tied to Iranian div, Berber and Sahelian spirit traditions, Indian South Asian Muslim folk practice, and Southeast Asian hantu/jin traditions.

timeline.event: Beginning of Quranic revelation; jinn appear in early Meccan revelations
timeline.significance: Establishes the Islamic doctrine of jinn

timeline.event: Al-Jāḥiẓ writes Kitāb al-Ḥayawān (Book of Animals), with extensive treatment of jinn
Al-Damīrī's Ḥayāt al-ḥayawān al-kubrā synthesises traditions on jinn
Al-Suyūṭī compiles Lāqiṭ al-marjān fī aḥkām al-jānn, a hadith-based treatise on jinn
Antoine Galland publishes the first volume of Les Mille et une nuits in French
Galland adds the 'Aladdin and the Wonderful Lamp' tale to volumes IX–X of his translation, drawing on dictation by the Maronite Syrian traveller Ḥannā Diyāb
timeline.significance: Origin of the Western lamp-genie trope

timeline.event: Amira El-Zein publishes Islam, Arabs, and the Intelligent World of the Jinn (Syracuse UP)

history.modern_era: Belief in jinn remains mainstream across Sunni and Shi'a Islam. Practical expressions include the recitation of the Muʿawwidhātayn (Surahs 113 and 114) for protection, the practice of ruqyah for healing and exorcism, and a substantial popular literature in Arabic, Persian, Urdu, Malay, Indonesian, Turkish, and other languages. Anthropologists (Celia Rothenberg, Tanya Luhrmann) and religious-studies scholars (Amira El-Zein, Travis Zadeh) have produced major modern studies. Western horror cinema, comics, and games have produced a separate, often highly distorted, 'djinn' character that bears little resemblance to the religious tradition.

documentary.name: Sūrat al-Jinn (Q. 72)
documentary.description: Surah of the Quran specifically devoted to the jinn, including their hearing of the Prophet's recitation and conversion to Islam.
documentary.analysis: Foundational scriptural text for the Islamic doctrine of jinn.
documentary.source: Quran 72; classical and modern Arabic and English editions

documentary.name: Kitāb al-Ḥayawān (al-Jāḥiẓ)
documentary.description: Encyclopaedic Abbasid-era treatise on animals that includes extensive material on jinn.

documentary.name: Les Mille et une nuits (Antoine Galland)
documentary.description: First European translation of the One Thousand and One Nights; introduces the 'génie' to Western literature, including the Aladdin tale dictated by Ḥannā Diyāb.

paranormal.name: Real created beings (Islamic doctrine)
paranormal.description: Within Islamic theology, the jinn are real created beings, made of fire, who live alongside humans, possess free will, and are accountable to God.
proponents: Mainstream Sunni and Shi'a Islamic theology

skeptical.name: Anthropological / religious-studies framing
skeptical.description: Jinn-belief functions as a culturally elaborated explanatory and therapeutic framework for misfortune, illness, dreams, and unusual experience. Cross-cultural anthropological work (Celia Rothenberg, Tanya Luhrmann) treats jinn-beliefs as a serious religious and cultural phenomenon without committing to their ontology.

skeptical.name: Western literary distortion
skeptical.description: The 'genie of the lamp' / 'three wishes' figure of European literature and Disney film bears only a distant relationship to Islamic jinn doctrine.
evidence_cited: Source-critical study of the Galland Nights

traditions: Folk Islam across the Maghreb, Sahel, Levant, Iran, South Asia, and Southeast Asia
stories: The conversion of a band of jinn (Q. 72)
Tales of jinn lovers and jinn marriages in the Thousand and One Nights
folklore.beliefs: Belief in jinn is a normative element of mainstream Islamic faith. Practices include recitation of protective surahs, taʿawwudh (seeking refuge in God), use of amulets (taʿāwidh), and ruqyah for possession.

indigenous.significance: Central to Islamic religious life; treat with the seriousness due to a living religious belief, not as 'fantasy creatures'.
indigenous.sensitivity_note: The Western 'genie' / 'wish-granting spirit' is a literary distortion. Jinn-belief is a living article of Islamic doctrine for over a billion people; framing should respect this.
indigenous.respect_guidelines: Distinguish carefully between the Islamic doctrine of jinn, regional folk practice, and the Western literary 'genie'.
